page_text:
130 THIRTY-NINTH REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION, 
It is believed that in view of his qualifications and experience in this line of 
work it would be in the interest of the service to make him permanent in his 
present position. 
April 28, 1922. . 
Mr. Sims Ely, of Arizona, may be appointed to the position of chief clerk 
and administrative assistant, Department of Justice, without reference to the 
civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General, who 
states that the position of chief clerk is highly confidential and requires a 
peculiar order of talent; that a diligent effort has been made within the classi￾fied service to find some one possessing the required qualifications, but without 
success. The Attorney General believes that Mr. Ely is especially qualified 
for the position and that the interests of the service would be promoted by 
exempting the appointment. 
May 20, 1922. ; 
Mr. John E. Pitts may be reinstated to a position in the Railway Mail Service 
without regard to time limit. 
He was appointed in the Railway Mail Service September 27, 1889, and 
served continuously therein until May 2, 1903, when his resignation was ac￾cepted, for the reason that, having been severely injured on duty in a railroad 
wreck a year previous to that time and having been granted all the leave of 
absence with pay allowed by law, he was still unable to resume duty. His reinstatement is recommended by the Postmaster General in order 
that he may be given such work in the Railway Mail Service as he will be able 
to perform. 
May 24, 1922. 
The following-named employees in the Office of the Superintendent, State, 
War, and Navy Department Buildings, are transferred from an unclassified to 
a classified status without regard to the provision of civil-service rules: William 
A. Boyd, Martha Jones, Malvina Lee, Anna M. Over, John A. Simms, Lillie B. 
Sinclair, and Susan Wills. 
This order is issued on the joint recommendation of the Commission in 
Charge of the State, War, and Navy Department Buildings, Lieut. Col. C. O. 
Sherrill, Superintendent of the State, War, and Navy Department Buildings, 
and the Civil Service Commission, because of the employees’ long, faithful, 
and efficient service, and for the reason that they are unable to pass the required 
civil-service examinations for lack of education and training. 
May 24, 1922. 
The following-named employee in the Office of Public Buildings and Grounds, 
is on the joint recommendation of the Secretary of War and of the Civil Service 
Commission transferred from an unclassified to a classified status without 
regard to the provision of the civil-service rules: John Miller, laborer. 
This order is issued on account of this employee’s long, faithful, and efficient 
service, and for the reason that he is unable to pass the required civil-service examination due to lack of education. 
May 24, 1922. 
Mrs. John E. Stephens may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified 
service without examination under the civil service rules. This order is 
issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, who states that she 
is the widow of Brig. Gen. John KE. Stephens, who died of pneumonia, in 
France, on January 4, 1919. He further states that she has been serving sat￾isfactorily as a temporary clerk, requiring a knowledge of the French language, 
in the Quartermaster Department at large, Fort Myer, Va.; and that the 
Quartermaster General reports that she has demonstrated the necessary quali￾fications for this work to a marked degree and that her permanent appointment 
would be to the best interests of the service. 
June 2, 1922. 
Mrs. Gertrude W. Kidd may be appointed to a clerical position in the classi￾fied service of the Government without regard to the requirements of the civil 
service rules.
next_page_text:

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 131 
Mrs. Kidd has been serving temporarily as a clerk in the Division of Rural 
Mails, Bureau of the Fourth Assistant Postmaster General, Post Office Depart￾ment, since August 12, 1918, and is the sole support of a blind, crippled son and 
an aged father. The Pgst Office Department reports that her work is satis￾factory and that it can continue to use her services if a civil service status can 
be procured for her. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the 
Acting Postmaster General. 
June 16, 1922. 
Mrs. Beulah T. Davis may be appointed to a clerical position in the classi￾fied service without examination under the civil-service rules. This order is 
issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the Director 
of the Coast and Geodetic Survey, who state that Mrs. Davis’ husband must 
now, at the age of 80 years, be retired for physical disability after 62 years 
of efficient and faithful service in the Coast and Geodetic Survey; that he 
has been unable to accumulate a competence for his remaining years; that Mrs. 
Davis was employed during the war in the Bureau of War Risk Insurance and 
there demonstrated her capacity satisfactorily to perform work similar in 
character to that which it is proposed to assign her; and that they believe 
her appointment is fully justified in the interests of good administration. 
July 14, 1922. 
The rule prohibiting the promotion of messenger girls to apportioned posi￾tions is waived to permit the promotion of Miss Elsie M. Robertson in the 
Department of Agriculture from messenger girl to clerk. 
Miss Robertson’s services have been highly satisfactory. The Secretary of 
Agriculture recommends the issuance of an Executive order permitting the 
promotion for exceptional reasons. 
The Civil Service Commission did not concur in recommending this order. 
July 31, 1922. 
Louis Vallone may be reinstated as an opener and packer in the customs 
service without reference to the length of time he has been separated from 
the service. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, 
who states that Mr. Vallone’s services were discontinued on January 31, 1916, 
under charges without sufficient evidence, after a service of more than 22 years, 
and it is believed his reinstatement will be in the interest of the service. 
The Civil Service Commission concurred in recommending the issuance of 
this order. 
August 28, 1922.

Mr. Shelley, after serving many years in the classified service of the Engineer Department, was furloughed without pay on September 30, 1911, and has been serving since September 7, 1917, with an excepted status. ; This order is recommended by the Secretary of War and the Civil Service Com- mission. 
February 26, 1923. 
Mr. George H. Woodson may be appointed to a clerical position in the Treasury 
Department without examination under the civil-service rules. . The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
February 26, 1923. 
Capt. William M. Hanson may be appointed to a position as immigrant inspector An i classified service of the Department of Labor without regard to the civil-service rules. This order is recommended by the Secretary of Labor because of the need on the Mexican border of the services of a man particularly familiar with local conditions and methods in order to secure the administration of the immigration laws on the border as applying to the surreptitious entry of aliens. Captain Hanson was for many years United States marshal for the Southern District of Texas, in which capacity he had charge of 500 miles of the border and as head of and in charge of the ranger forces of the State of Texas he has become thoroughly familiar with the particular problems presented. Because of Captain Hanson’s experience, which peculiarly qualifies him for the duties of the position of immigration inspector on the Mexican border, and because the register of eligibles is depleted the Civil Service Commission joins with the Secre- tary of Labor in recommending this order. 
March 5, 1923. 
Mrs. Helen Carrick may be reinstated as a clerk in the Treasury Department without 
reference to the length of time she has been separated from the service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mrs. Carrick was employed as a clerk in the Treasury Department for a Poriod of almost two years and rendered satisfactory service while so employed. er husband, who served overseas and was in the battles of the Argonne, Lagny, Seille, and St. Mihiel, was recently killed in an automobile accident, leaving her with a 2-year-old child to support. Livi Civil Service Commission is unable to concur in the recommendation for this order. 
April 9, 1923. 
Mrs. Maude Morrison may be appointed to a clerical position in the Treasury Depart- ment without regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mrs. Morrison is the wife of George R. Morrison, who served for 17 years in the Treasury Department and 4 years in the Marine Corps of the United States, and whose failing health caused his retirement from the service upon a small annuity. The Civil Service Commission did not concur in recommending this order. 
April 9, 1923. 
Miss Nancy Taylor may be appointed clerk in the classified service of the War Department without examination. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of War, who states that Miss Taylor has been employed 15 months in an excepted position in the War Depart- ment and during that petiod has acquired an experience and developed a capacity in certain special work which will make it to the interest of the department to retain her in the classified service. The Civil Service Commission is unable to concur in recommending this order. 
April 9, 1923. 
Mr. Green A. Stephens may be reinstated in an appropriate position in the Post Office Service on condition that he waive his claim to annuity upon retirement. Mr. Stephens was removed from the position of letter carrier on April 12, 1905, on charges which upon reinvestigation were found to be untrue. Hisreinstatement wasauthorized by an Executive order of August 26, 1915, but, for private reasons, it was impossible for him to reenter the service at that time. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order.

April 14, 1923. 
Miss Alice Robertson may be appointed to the position of welfare worker in the United Stars Veterans’ Bureau without reference to the requirements of the civil service rules. 
May 5, 1923. 
Mr. Henry T. Ellington may be reinstated to the position of clerk in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Ellington was removed from the position of clerk in the Railway Mail Service on May 17, 1916, charged with embezzlement. The Postmaster General states that he was tried and acquitted of the charge, that a most careful investigation has con- vinced him that Mr. Ellington’s removal was an injustice and that he was entirely innocent of the charges made against him, and that his reinstatement by Executive order would serve the public interest better than the appointment of a new clerk. The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
May 22, 1923. : 
Mr. Daniel R. Edwards may be appointed a contact representative in the United States Veterans’ Bureau without examination under the civil service rules. Mr. Edwards is a permanently disabled beneficiary of the Veterans’ Bureau through the lossofan arm and aleg. He hasbeen decorated with the distinguished service crossand twice with the congressional medal of honor. The director of the Veterans’ Bureau recommended Mr. Edwards’ appointment, as he has been on trial and has given evidence that he can render good service. The director regards the case as exceptional, in that the appointment would have a favor- able psychological effect upon disabled ex-service men because of Mr. Edwards’ own disability and his clear conception of vocational work, gained through his own training, and because of the association he has had with welfare ex-service men’s organizations. The Civil Service Commission concurred in this recommendation.

expected_title: [Regulationsgoverning the employment of unskilledlab orers outside Washington, D. C] Regulation VIII on reinstatement, amended. 1923 CSR 154.
page_text:
EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 155 
(b) A person honorably released from the active military or naval service of the United States after service in the Civil War, War with Spain, or War with Germany, or his widow, or an Army nurse of any war, may be reinstated, if physically qualified, within five years from the date of separation from his unclassified position; or, if a person served in the War with Germany, he may be reinstated within five years from the date of his honorable discharge from the military or naval service. - {e) The widow of a veteran of the War with Germany formerly in the unclassified service, who was the wife of such veteran while he was in the military service, may “be reinstated within five years from the date of cessation of her husband’s military service by death or otherwise without discredit. d) A person separated from an unclassified position in the field service may be reemployed in the same office within one year without certificate. 
ORDERS EXCEPTING PERSONS NAMED FROM THE REQUIREMENTS OF THE RULES. 
November 18, 1922. 
Frank C. Staley has a classified status in the field service of the Veterans’ Bureau under the civil-service law as result of open competitive examination. The require- ment of six months’ service as a classified employee before transfer is hereby waived to permit Mr. Staley’s transfer from the Veterans’ Bureau to the Post Office Depart￾ment. 
December 30, 1922. 
# Mrs. Anna M. Curran may be reappointed as printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing of the Treasury Department. She served in this position from September 15, 1919, when she was appointed without examination under author- ity of an Executive order of January 15, 1918, until August 13, 1921, when she was furloughed because of reduction of force, her furlough being largely due to the fact that her husband was employed in the Government service. Since her furlough she has been left a widow by the assassination of her husband. She received several bullet wounds in trying to protect him. She has been out of the service too long to be eligible for reemployment, and the Executive order under which she received Shpoigimeit has been revoked. She could have remained in the service indefinitely if no occasion had arisen to require her separation. In view of all the circumstances the Secretary of the Treasury recommends her reinstatement. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation that she be reap- pointed with the same status she would have had if she had remained in the service under her original appointment. 
January 8, 1923. 
Mrs. Frank L. Scott may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service of the War Department without regard to the civil-service rules. This order is recommended by the Chief of Finance, under whom Mrs. Scott served under temporary appointment. She has performed her duties in a satisfactory manner and by her general aptitude has become a valuable asset to the service. Her husband is confined in St. Elizabeths Hospital suffering from paresis and his recovery is hope- less, this condition doubtless having resulted largely from his service as a soldier in the Tropics and to overwork during the late war. While in the Tropics he contracted a fever, which caused a generally weakened condition of his system. During the war he organized an important unit of the War Department in Washington and gave attention to his work without regard to hours. Mrs. Scott has been left solely upon her own resources, as her husband receives no pension or other remuneration. The Secretary of War, while reluctant to recommend an Executive order, states 
that favorable action will be agreeable to him. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
February 20, 1923. 
Mrs. Mildred L. Jennings may be appointed to a clerical position in the General Accounting Office without regard to the civil-service rules. 
This order is recommended by the Comptroller General, who has known Mrs, Jennings for many years, has supervised her work, and whose services, because of her dependability and qualifications, can be used to advantage on a particular work about which he feels some concern. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
February 26, 1923. 
Mr. Thomas S. Shelley may be reinstated with a classified status effective September 7, 1917.

He helped to identify the thieves when they were arrested and was many times threatened by their friends. He has been employed as a temporary laborer since June 1, 1921. Examinations have been held by the Civil Service Commission, but no eligibles have been obtained. Mr. Williams is 58 years of age and did not take the examination, as persons more than 45 years of age are not appointed in the Postal Service. The Civil Service Commission concurred in the recommendation. 
June 18, 1923. 
Mrs. Amelia V. Briscoe may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service without examination. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of War, who states that Mrs. Briscoe is the widow of Capt. William J. Briscoe, Philippine Scouts, who lost his life last year in the Philippines from burns caused while fighting fire in an attempt to save the lives of soldiers. Mrs. Briscoe was temporarily appointed without examination in the Bureau of Pen- sions under an act of Congress which permitted temporary appointments to be made without regard to the civil service rules. It is reported that her work is above the average and that she has faithfully and conscientiously discharged all the duties of the osition. P The Civil Service Commission did not concur in the issuance of this order. 
June 19, 1928. 
Mr. George E. Strong, of Kansas, may be appointed to the position of chief clerk and pdminisisive assistant, Department of Justice, without reference to the civil service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General, who states that the position of chief clerk is highly confidential and requires a peculiar order of talent; that a diligent effort has been made within the classified service to find some one possessing the required qualifications, but without success. The Attorney General believes that Mr. Strong is especially qualified for the position and that the interests of the service would be promoted by exempting the appointment.
